To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of the gregarious parasitoid E. pennicornus significantly reduced the levels damage incurred by the pest L. oleraceo on both control and GNA-expressin plants and that GNA expression by potato plants did not affect the ability of E. pennicornu to parasitise or subsequently reproduce.
The expression of a snowdrop lectin gene in potato plants reduced the level of feeding by the noctuid pest, Lacanobia oeracea, when compared to control potato plants.

the presence of the gregarious endoparasitoid, Eulophus penicornis, significantly reduced the level damage caused to transgenic and non-transgenic potato plants by the pest species, Lacanobia ooleracea, and that this wasp was able to develop successfully on larvae reared on transgenic potato plants expressing the snowdrop lectin, Galanthus nivali agglutinin (GNA).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of transgenic potato plants which express the gene encoding snow drop lectin (Galantus nivalis Agglutinin, or GNA) in the hope of reducing the levels of damage caused by potato aphids, and other pest species, and thereby reducing the need for chemical insecticides.
the development of a sustainable approach to pest control, which combines transgenic plants expressing a novel insecticidal protein and a natural enemy.
the potential for the use of transgenics in integrated pest management strategies and the development of transgenic crops with enhanced resistance to insect pests and diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of GNA by transgenic potato does not affect the ability of the parasitoids to parasitise the host or develop into adults.
the presence of the transgenic plant and the parasitoid together resulted in a 21% reduction in damage caused by the insect pest.
transgenic plants expressing snowdrop lectin can be used in conjunction with the parasitoid to reduce damage by the pest species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of insecticidal transgenic plants expressing GNA can be used in conjunction with the biological control agent E. pennicorn.
the expression of insecticidal proteins in plants does not affect the ability of beneficial insects to control pest insects, but can augment their effectiveness.
the presence of E. pennicornus in the glasshouse trials reduced pest damage by 21% in GNA-express plants, and 14% in the control plants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of insecticidal proteins by plants may be used as a tool to augment the efficacy of beneficial insects.
the use of GNA expressing plants may provide a means of augmenting the biocontrol activity of parasitoids.
the use of insecticidal plants may not only reduce the damage caused by pest insects but may also increase the effectiveness of beneficial insects.
